messages.content: What are tokens and why do they cost money?

Tokens are how AI models read text. 1 token ≈ 4 characters. They directly drive costs. For example, summarizing a 50-page document = 1000 input tokens + 200 output tokens = $0.00013 per request. At scale with 1000 requests/day = $130/day = $4000/month. This is why token optimization is critical. You can reduce costs by: 1) Optimizing inputs, 2) Constraining outputs, 3) Model tiering, 4) Caching, 5) Batch processing. Key insight: Tokens are the cost lever. Control them, control your economics.
Explain the latency-quality-cost tradeoff in AI systems.

Every AI decision is a triangle. You can optimize for 2 of 3: quality, latency, or cost. Example: Gemini Flash is 0.5 sec and cheap but good quality. Gemini Pro is 2 sec, excellent quality, 10x more expensive. Claude Opus is 3 sec, exceptional, 20x more expensive. We chose Flash because users tolerate 0.5s latency, quality is acceptable, and cost is manageable. But the tradeoff changes by context. For premium products use Pro/Opus. For critical latency use Flash. For cost-sensitive use Flash with optimization. The PM skill: Understand the constraint that matters most, then optimize for 2 of 3.
You're building a summarization feature for a banking app. Which model would you choose and why?

My choice depends on the specific use case. For customer-facing real-time chat: use Gemini Flash because customers expect <1 second response. For document review by loan officers: use Claude Sonnet because accuracy is critical and officers can wait 2-3 seconds. For regulatory reporting: use Claude Opus plus manual review because legal liability is high. My approach: 1) Define the SLA first, 2) Run A/B test with 2-3 models on real data, 3) Measure latency and quality, 4) Choose based on data, 5) Iterate quarterly. Don't guess. Measure. Decide.
How would you handle a bad summary from your AI system?

Bad summaries destroy trust. I'd implement multiple layers: Prevention: Use better models for high-stakes situations, write detailed prompts with examples. Detection: Let users rate summaries with thumbs up/down, measure ROUGE scores, flag low confidence. Transparency: Show citations from source text, display confidence scores, let users review original. Recovery: Offer regenerate with different model, show alternative summaries, escalate to human review. For banking, never let decisions be solely based on AI. Always require human review and maintain audit trail. The key insight: Don't assume the AI is right. Always give users ability to verify and override.
Explain the difference between Stage 1 (Summarization) and Stage 2 (RAG).

Stage 1 Summarization: User uploads document, AI reads all 50 pages, outputs summary. Cost is $0.00013 per request. Can't have follow-up conversation. Stage 2 RAG: Split document into chunks, retrieve relevant chunks, summarize. User can ask follow-up questions. Cost per request: $0.00008, 33% cheaper. Accuracy improves from 85% to 90%. Stage 1 is stateless, Stage 2 is stateful. When to use: Stage 1 for one-off summaries, Stage 2 for conversations and follow-ups. Key difference: Stage 2 remembers your documents through embeddings and vector database.
What are embeddings and why do they matter for RAG?

Embeddings convert text to numbers. Similar text gets similar numbers. Example: Interest rate text → [0.2, -0.5, 0.8...], What's the rate text → [0.19, -0.51, 0.79...], very similar! RAG without embeddings requires reading entire document every time. With embeddings: Convert question to numbers, search vector database for top-3 similar chunks in milliseconds. Cost impact: Without embeddings = $0.00075 per query. With embeddings = $0.00006 per query. 12x cheaper! Embedding quality matters. Better embeddings = better matching. Key insight: Embeddings make semantic search possible. Without them, RAG doesn't work.
Explain vector databases and why they're better than regular databases for RAG.

Regular SQL databases excel at exact matches. Vector databases excel at similarity search. Example: SQL says no match for interest rate question. Vector DB finds it instantly because it understands meaning. Options: ChromaDB for prototypes, FAISS for scale, Pinecone for managed service. Cost: ChromaDB free, FAISS free, Pinecone $30-100/month. Real example: Bank has 10K documents. Without vector DB = read 1000 pages per query. With vector DB = read 3 relevant pages per query. 333x faster! Vector DB uses cosine similarity: 1.0 = identical, 0.5 = similar, 0.0 = unrelated. Key insight: Vector DB is core of RAG. Without it, RAG is just slow sequential search.
Design a RAG system for a banking customer support chatbot.

Requirements: 500 internal documents, real-time responses <3 sec, 95% accuracy. Architecture: 1) Ingest documents daily, 2) Chunk into 500 tokens with 100 token overlap, 3) Create embeddings, 4) Store in FAISS vector DB, 5) Retrieve top-3 chunks on query, 6) Pass to Claude Sonnet for generation. Cost: $64/month. Success metrics: Response time <3s p95, 95% accuracy, 80% adoption, CSAT 4.2+. Failure modes: If wrong chunks retrieved, use better embedding model. If hallucination despite good chunks, use Claude or reduce temperature. If latency high, cache frequent questions. If cost exceeds budget, reduce document count or use cheaper model. Key: RAG is only as good as your source documents. Clean them first.
How would you improve RAG quality? Give me 5 levers.

Lever 1 Retrieval Quality: Better chunking, better embedding model, retrieve more chunks, add reranking. Lever 2 Prompt Engineering: Add role-playing, constraints, examples. Same model, 50% better quality. Lever 3 Model Quality: Use better LLM. Flash=85% quality, Pro=92%, Sonnet=94%, Opus=97%. Lever 4 Context Quality: Remove outdated docs, add metadata, resolve contradictions. Lever 5 Human Feedback: Users flag bad answers, analyze why, retrain. Most teams improve Levers 4 and 2 first, not the fancy stuff. Measurement: Track for every 100 questions, how many rated accurate? Target 95%+. If lower, diagnose which lever is bottleneck and fix that first.
Should we use RAG or fine-tuning? How do I decide?

Use RAG if: Launch in <3 months, documents change frequently, budget <$500/month, 90% accuracy acceptable. Use fine-tuning if: Need 95%+ accuracy, domain is specialized, budget allows $5K+, have 1000+ training examples. Hybrid is best: Fine-tune model on your data (learns patterns), use RAG to retrieve fresh documents. Cost comparison: RAG only = $50/month, Fine-tuning = $5K upfront + $100/month, Hybrid = $500/month. Timeline: RAG = 6 weeks, Fine-tuning = 12 weeks, Hybrid = 12 weeks. Decision framework: What's your accuracy requirement? How often does data change? What's your budget? How much training data do you have? Most teams start with RAG, validate market, then invest in fine-tuning if needed.
How do you handle contradictions in RAG when documents conflict?

Problem: Old policy says 5% rate, new says 3%. Both in RAG. Which wins? Solution phase 1: Every document has version, effective_date, author. Build dependency graph. Keep only current, valid docs. Phase 2: Detect conflicts using LLM. Create conflict index. Phase 3: On retrieval, if conflict detected, apply rule: use newest version. Show both old and new with explanation. Phase 4: Confidence scoring. No conflict = 95% confidence. Conflict = 60% confidence, flag for human review. Real example: Bank has 5 different Loan Policy docs. Solution: Keep only 2024 policy, archive others. When users ask, RAG retrieves only current policy. Key: Don't put contradictory docs in RAG. Clean up first. If genuine ambiguity (different branch policies), show all versions and ask user to clarify.
Design an AI summary system for a law firm with 10,000 legal documents.

High-stakes requirements: 10K legal docs, lawyers need <5 sec summaries, 98% accuracy mandatory, audit trail required. Architecture: 8 layers. Layer 1 Ingestion: Batch upload, quality check, versioning. Layer 2 Processing: Chunk 500-1000 tokens, overlap 100, lawyer-friendly chunking by sections. Layer 3 Storage: FAISS for speed, metadata tracking. Layer 4 Retrieval: Top-10 chunks, rerank, select top-3. Layer 5 Generation: Claude Opus (best quality), temperature 0.2 (precise). Layer 6 Quality Gates: Check if summary supported by source, highlight risks, confidence score. Layer 7 Output: Summary with citations, risk flags, deadlines, confidence. Layer 8 Audit: Immutable log of every access for 7-year retention. Cost: <$50/month. Success: 98% accuracy, <3s p95, 70% adoption, 4.5+ CSAT. Legal-specific: Citations mandatory, confidence thresholds, red flag detection, multiple review layers. Key: In legal, trust is everything. Never assume AI is right. Always show work and maintain audit trail.
If you could only optimize ONE thing in your AI system, what would it be?

I would optimize MEASUREMENT, not model quality, not latency, not cost. Why? Most teams optimize the wrong thing because they don't measure first. Example: Team A optimizes latency 2s→1s. Costs $50K. Result: Users don't care. They want quality, not speed. Team B measures first: 80% feedback is quality issues. Optimizes quality. Costs $20K. Result: 15% higher retention, $100K more revenue. The difference: Team B measured first. Measurement framework: Tier 1 Operational: latency p95, error rate, uptime, cost per request. Tier 2 User: adoption, retention, satisfaction, quality. Tier 3 Business: revenue, conversion, churn, LTV. What to measure: Every request logs timestamp, user, model, latency, cost, quality, user rating. A/B test hypotheses. Measure before and after. Decision should be data-driven, not gut-feel. The insight: If you optimize without measuring, you're flying blind and wrong 80% of the time. With measurement, you're right 80% of the time. That's the 10x difference.
